title: French Omelette
description: A pale, smooth omelette rolled into an oval, just set outside and soft inside, with no browning. Jacques Pépin's La Technique (1976) taught kitchen skills through step-by-step photographs, and he has shown this classic omelette on television beside a browned country-style one, including in the PBS American Masters film Jacques Pépin: The Art of Craft (2017).
notes:
Inspired by Jacques Pépin, *La Technique* (1976). Written for Sous; not his recipe.

The whole thing takes about a minute in the pan, so have the plate, butter and chives ready first. Your first few may tear or brown; they still taste good, and making several in a row is the quickest way to learn the feel.

For a filled omelette, scatter a little grated Gruyère, sautéed mushrooms or ham across the middle just before folding.
ingredients: 1 tablespoon (14 g) unsalted butter, plus a little extra for brushing
steps: Crack the eggs into a bowl with the salt and pepper and beat with a fork for about 30 seconds, until completely blended with no streaks of white.
Set an 8-inch (20 cm) nonstick or well-seasoned carbon steel pan over medium heat. Add the butter and swirl until it foams and the foam starts to subside. It should not brown.

Pour in the eggs. At once stir them with the flat of a fork or a heatproof spatula while shaking the pan back and forth, keeping the eggs moving so they form very small curds. After 30 to 45 seconds they should look like loose, wet scrambled eggs.
Stop stirring and spread the eggs into an even layer. Leave for 10 to 15 seconds so the bottom sets into a thin skin; the top should still be moist. Scatter over the chives.
Tilt the pan away from you and fold the near third of the omelette toward the centre. Tap the handle so the omelette slides to the far edge of the pan.

Hold the plate against the far edge and turn the pan over so the omelette rolls onto the plate seam side down. Tidy the shape with a paper towel if needed, brush with a little butter for shine, and eat right away.
